name: Chrome
basis: reflection mapping on a brightness height field (how; hist: Blinn and Newell 1976)
note: Imitates a mirror material, not plating.

lumenary.blurb: Your picture cast in liquid metal: bright parts rise, and the surface mirrors a sky and a horizon.

facts.bestOn: Pictures with smooth shapes and bright highlights

why: Chrome is a mirror, so what you see in it is the room around it, not the object. To fake that, brightness is treated as a height map, bright parts are hills, and each pixel looks up a different part of an imaginary sky: dark overhead, bright near the horizon, then a darker ground. Steeper slopes reflect other parts of the sky, and that is what makes the metal look liquid.
how: Mix two blurs of different size, so shapes are smooth but keep some fine detail.
Read the slope of the map to get a surface normal, an arrow pointing out of the surface.
Work out the reflected direction, and use its up and down part to choose a position on a strip that stands for the world.
Shift where flat areas land on the strip with the horizon slider.
Add a small hard highlight from a light at the top left. Gold and cobalt use different strips.
history: Chrome trim defined cars of the 1950s. In computer graphics, James Blinn and Martin Newell described reflection mapping in 1976, the method of looking up a surrounding picture from a surface’s angle. The liquid metal villain of the film Terminator 2 in 1991 brought the look to a worldwide audience.
uses: Poster and title lettering with a metal finish
terms: A unit arrow pointing straight out of a surface.
A picture of the surroundings that a shiny surface reflects.
A small bright spot where a surface mirrors a light.
paragraphs: Chrome is a mirror, so what you see in it is not the object but the room around it. To fake that, the picture’s brightness is treated as a height map: bright parts are hills. Two blurs of different size are mixed so the shapes are smooth but still have some fine detail. The slope of the map at each pixel gives a surface normal, a unit arrow that points out of the surface; the steeper the slope, the more the arrow leans.

A leaning surface reflects a different part of the sky. The reflected direction is worked out from the normal, and its up-and-down part chooses a position on a strip that stands for the world: dark sky overhead, a bright band near the horizon, a hard edge where the horizon is, then a darker ground and a light floor. The “horizon” slider shifts where flat areas land on the strip. A small, hard highlight, a specular spot from a light at the top left, is added on top. Gold and cobalt use different strips.

equations.note: Height map: two box blurs of radius r and r/3 mixed.
Normal from the Sobel slopes G (k grows with the relief slider) and the sideways part of the mirror direction for a viewer looking straight down.
Position on the environment strip (0 top, 1 bottom); η is the horizon slider.
The highlight; m is halfway between the light direction and the viewer.

presets.text: Gold with deep relief looks like a cast medal.
Cobalt with lower smoothness has more crisp, electric ridges.
Switch off the sharp gleam for a satin finish.
